title: Stanford Professor Easha Anand Elected to American Law Institute
excerpt: The Indian-American law professor and Supreme Court litigator joins the prestigious legal body that has shaped American law for nearly a century.
body:
• Easha Anand, a Stanford Law School professor who grew up partly in India, has been elected to the American Law Institute (ALI), joining 27 other current or emeriti Stanford Law faculty in the organization
  • Anand co-directs Stanford's Supreme Court Litigation Clinic, where she has won unanimous decisions before the nation's highest court on behalf of workers, criminal defendants, and civil rights plaintiffs
  • She clerked for Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor and was among 49 new members elected to the ALI, which drafts influential Restatements of the Law and Model Codes
  • The election recognizes Anand's work as an expert on Supreme Court practice, civil rights, and prisoners' rights

Stanford Law School professor Easha Anand, who grew up partly in India and partly in suburban Washington, has been elected to the American Law Institute, one of the most influential legal organizations in the United States. Anand is among 49 new members elected to the body, which has shaped American law through its Restatements, Model Codes, and Principles of Law since its founding nearly a century ago.

Anand co-directs Stanford Law School's Supreme Court Litigation Clinic, where she represents employees, noncitizens, consumers, unions, criminal defendants, and civil rights plaintiffs before the U.S. Supreme Court. Her election to the ALI recognizes her as a leading voice in Supreme Court practice and civil rights law.

A Record of Supreme Court Victories

Anand's case portfolio at Stanford reads like a catalog of landmark civil rights battles. Her recent victories include cases brought on behalf of a long-distance truck driver who was deceived into purchasing a product containing a federally controlled substance, a jeweler who was jailed after police fabricated evidence against him, and a whistleblower fired for reporting securities-law violations — the last resulting in a unanimous Supreme Court decision.

"ALI has played an extraordinary role in shaping American law by bringing together judges, practitioners, and scholars to work through difficult legal questions with rigor and care. I'm honored to join that community, including many Stanford Law colleagues, and look forward to contributing to its work."

— Easha Anand, Stanford Law School

Before joining the Stanford faculty in 2023, Anand served as Supreme Court and appellate counsel at the MacArthur Justice Center, where she litigated police excessive force, prison conditions, wrongful conviction, and other criminal defense and civil rights cases. At one point, she represented a man who had been held in solitary confinement for nearly three decades. While the Supreme Court denied review in that case, an extensive media campaign led to his release into the general prison population.

From India to the Supreme Court Bar

Anand's path to the top of American legal practice took her from India and suburban Washington to Yale University for her undergraduate degree, then to the University of California, Berkeley School of Law. After graduating in 2014, she clerked for Judge Paul J. Watford on the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals and then for Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor — one of the most sought-after clerkships in the American legal profession.

She worked as an associate at Orrick Herrington & Sutcliffe before joining the MacArthur Justice Center and eventually Stanford. Her academic colleagues have noted her journalistic and investigative background as a distinctive asset in legal practice.

At Stanford, Anand has emphasized the importance of using the university's resources and prestige on behalf of those with fewer resources. The clinic's only limiting principle, she has said, is that it represents "the less resourced side of the v" — whether that means a worker challenging a corporation or a noncitizen facing the U.S. government.

What the ALI Election Means

The American Law Institute's work carries significant weight in American courts and legislatures. The Restatements of the Law it produces are regularly cited by judges, and its Model Codes have formed the basis for legislation across the country. Membership is by election and reserved for judges, lawyers, and academics who have demonstrated exceptional expertise.

Anand joins 27 other current or emeriti Stanford Law faculty who are ALI members. UC Berkeley Law professor Seth Davis and three Berkeley Law alumni were also elected in the same cohort, reflecting the strong representation of Indian-American legal scholars at the institute.

For the Indian-American legal community, Anand's election is the latest in a series of high-profile achievements. Her work at the intersection of criminal justice, civil rights, and Supreme Court practice positions her as one of the most prominent Indian-American legal advocates in the country.
